title: Repeated Games through a Cyclic Operator: A Golden-Ratio Threshold, Fractal Payoff Sets, and the Golden-Window Conjecture
abstract: In a discounted repeated game, the continuation values along a cyclic path of play are the fixed point of the linear operator x ↦ DQx + (I − D)p, with D = δI and Q a cyclic shift. This preprint uses that identity to study the symmetric n-player game in which a player whose k co-players cooperate earns k + 1 by cooperating and k + 2 by defecting. Main results: 1. The three-player rotation scheme, in which exactly one player defects in each period, is a subgame-perfect equilibrium path if and only if δ ≥ 1/φ ≈ 0.618, where φ is the golden ratio. For n players the threshold lies in (1/(n−2) − 2/(n−2)^n, 1/(n−2)). 2. The payoff vector (2, 4, 2) is never an equilibrium payoff. This corrects an example in the author's earlier preprint (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22058777). 3. With public randomization, (2+t, 4−t, 2+t) is an equilibrium payoff if and only if δ ≥ max(1/2, 1−t). 4. Without randomization, the set of sustainable t passes through three regimes: two points for 1/2 ≤ δ < 1/φ, a countably infinite set at δ = 1/φ, and the full segment for δ ≥ 2/3. Inside the window 1/φ < δ < 2/3 it has positive Hausdorff dimension, with an explicit lower bound. 5. Golden-window conjecture: inside the window the set has Lebesgue measure zero, and its dimension increases continuously from 0 to 1. Numerical evidence is reported. 6. In the linear dilemma with benefit b and cost c, the rotation is sustainable exactly when cooperation is efficient, the three-player threshold is (√(1 + 4c/b) − 1)/2, and the rotation always needs more patience than cooperation by everyone. The literature has not been searched systematically, and some of the results may be known. All proofs are given in full. This is a preprint and has not been peer-reviewed. Every number in the paper is produced by games/games.py and checked by verification/check_games.py in https://github.com/cpsbvbng26-dotcom/trinity-operator (MIT licence). title: Machine-mediated Rediscovery: A Case Study in Novelty, Priority, and Self-correction
abstract: A language model supplied the mathematical content of a short series of preprints that were presented as a new "framework". Less than a year later, the same author, now working with a different language model, established that the central operator was a special case of the Friedkin-Johnsen model of opinion dynamics, a standard model that the first preprint had itself named as a neighbouring field without citing any of its literature. The route from the first publication ran through nine recorded stages, the last three recorded contemporaneously, and ended in that identification. This paper uses the case to ask what existing frameworks in the philosophy and sociology of science can and cannot say about novelty claims when the generating step is performed by a machine. I argue that (i) the case is neither a Mertonian multiple nor a rediscovery in the usual sense, because the arrival was neither independent nor human; (ii) when generation moves outside the human agent, the context of justification must absorb a task that was previously distributed across both contexts, namely the search for priority; and (iii) the correction that followed is best read as epistemic iteration from a defective starting point, in which implementation, not reflection, exposed the error that mattered. The correction was itself carried out with a language model, and the record does not separate the human share from the machine's share at each step. The paper makes no claim of mathematical novelty.
